slides.title: A normal distribution
slides.body: A normal (Gaussian) distribution is continuous, symmetric, and bell shaped, with mean μ and standard deviation σ.
slides.question: What does moving μ change about the curve?

slides.title: Normal notation
slides.body: In this textbook, the second entry in N(μ,σ) is the standard deviation.
slides.question: For X~N(40,6), what are the mean and standard deviation?

slides.title: The standard normal
slides.body: The standard normal distribution has mean zero and standard deviation one.
slides.question: Where is the center of this distribution?

slides.title: A standardized value
slides.body: A z-score measures distance from the mean in standard deviations.
slides.question: What does a z-score of -1.5 tell us?

slides.title: A positive z-score
slides.body: Model: component lengths are normal with mean 40 mm and standard deviation 6 mm.
slides.question: What is the z-score for a length of 49 mm?

slides.title: A negative z-score
slides.body: Model: component lengths are normal with mean 40 mm and standard deviation 6 mm.
slides.question: What is the z-score for a length of 28 mm?

slides.title: At the mean
slides.body: Model: X is normal with mean 40 and standard deviation 6.
slides.question: What z-score belongs to X=40?

slides.title: Returning to original units
slides.body: A value can be recovered from its z-score, mean, and standard deviation.
slides.question: For μ=40 and σ=6, what value has z=-0.5?

slides.title: Comparing different scales
slides.body: Model A has mean 40 and SD 6. Model B has mean 100 and SD 12.
slides.question: Which is farther above its mean in standard deviations: A=49 or B=112?

slides.title: Scores are not probabilities
slides.body: A z-score describes standardized location.
slides.question: Why can z=2.5 be valid while a probability of 2.5 cannot?

slides.title: Standardizing an event
slides.body: Model: X~N(40,6).
slides.question: What standard-normal event corresponds to X<46?

slides.title: Symmetry
slides.body: The standard normal density is symmetric about zero.
slides.question: How does P(Z<-1.4) compare with P(Z>1.4)?

slides.title: The center divides the area
slides.body: Model: Z is standard normal.
slides.question: What is P(Z<0)?

slides.title: One standard deviation
slides.body: For a normal distribution, about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean.
slides.question: For μ=40 and σ=6, what interval contains that central region?

slides.title: Empirical Rule
slides.body: The Empirical Rule, or 68–95–99.7 rule, gives approximate central areas within one, two, and three normal standard deviations.
slides.question: For μ = 40 and σ = 6, what endpoints enclose the middle 99.7%?

slides.title: Two standard deviations
slides.body: For a normal distribution, about 95% of values lie within two standard deviations of the mean.
slides.question: Approximately what proportion lies above μ+2σ?

slides.title: Three standard deviations
slides.body: For a normal distribution, about 99.7% of values lie within three standard deviations of the mean.
slides.question: Approximately what proportion lies outside that interval?

slides.title: Areas between standard deviations
slides.body: Use the 68–95–99.7 rule for a normal distribution.
slides.question: What percentage lies between one and two standard deviations above the mean?

slides.title: Using a cumulative table
slides.body: A standard-normal table may report area to the left of z.
slides.question: If its entry for z=1.2 is 0.8849, what is P(Z>1.2)?

slides.title: A negative cumulative cutoff
slides.body: Given: P(Z<1.2)=0.8849 for a standard normal Z.
slides.question: What is P(Z<-1.2)?

slides.title: Normality matters
slides.body: Synthetic data have a long right tail and several unusually large values.
slides.question: Would calculating z-scores alone justify standard-normal probability calculations?

slides.title: Location versus shape
slides.body: Standardization subtracts a mean and divides by a positive standard deviation.
slides.question: Would standardizing a strongly skewed variable make its distribution normal?

slides.title: Defining the variable
slides.body: Model: package masses are approximately normal with mean 500 g and standard deviation 20 g.
slides.question: What does X represent if we select one package?

slides.title: A lower-tail probability
slides.body: Area to the left of a cutoff gives a lower-tail probability. Model: X ~ N(500,20), in grams.
slides.question: What is the probability that one package weighs less than 480 g?

slides.title: An upper-tail probability
slides.body: Area to the right of a cutoff gives an upper-tail probability. Model: X ~ N(500,20), in grams.
slides.question: What is the probability that one package weighs more than 530 g?

slides.title: A probability between cutoffs
slides.body: Model: X~N(500,20), measured in grams.
slides.question: What is P(490<X<520)?

slides.title: Outside an acceptable range
slides.body: Model: package masses follow N(500,20). The accepted range is 470 to 530 g.
slides.question: What proportion falls outside the accepted range?

slides.title: Strict or inclusive?
slides.body: Model: exact package mass has a continuous normal distribution.
slides.question: Does P(X<480) differ from P(X≤480)?

slides.title: A technology input
slides.body: A normal cumulative probability tool needs a mean, standard deviation, and cutoff or interval.
slides.question: For P(X>530) when X~N(500,20), what information should you enter?

slides.title: Shading a normal probability
slides.body: Model: package mass X ~ N(500,20), in grams.
slides.question: How would you sketch and shade the region for P(490 < X < 520)?

slides.title: Checking the direction
slides.body: Model: X~N(500,20). A calculation for P(X>530) returns 0.9332.
slides.question: Is that result plausible for a cutoff above the mean?

slides.title: From probability to expected count
slides.body: Model: 8% of packages fall outside specification. A shipment contains 250 packages.
slides.question: How many out-of-specification packages should we expect?

slides.title: A percentile
slides.body: A percentile cutoff specifies area at or below that value.
slides.question: What probability equation defines the 90th percentile k?

slides.title: Finding a percentile
slides.body: Model: X~N(500,20), measured in grams.
slides.question: What mass is the 90th percentile?

slides.title: Inverse normal input
slides.body: An inverse normal calculation returns the cutoff for a specified area to its left. Model: X ~ N(500,20).
slides.question: What inputs find the mass exceeded by only 10% of packages?

slides.title: An upper-tail cutoff
slides.body: Model: X~N(500,20), measured in grams.
slides.question: Only 5% of packages exceed what mass?

slides.title: Critical value
slides.body: A critical value is a cutoff marking a specified probability region. Such cutoffs will be used in confidence intervals and tests.
slides.question: What standard-normal critical value leaves area 0.025 to its right?

slides.title: A lower-tail cutoff
slides.body: Model: X~N(500,20), measured in grams.
slides.question: What mass separates the lowest 10% from the rest?

slides.title: The middle 90%
slides.body: Model: X~N(500,20), measured in grams.
slides.question: What symmetric interval around the mean contains the middle 90%?

slides.title: Quartiles from a model
slides.body: Model: X~N(500,20), measured in grams.
slides.question: What masses are the first and third quartiles?

slides.title: An interquartile range
slides.body: Model: X~N(500,20), measured in grams.
slides.question: What is the model's interquartile range?

slides.title: Different spreads
slides.body: Model A is N(500,10). Model B is N(500,20), with mass in grams.
slides.question: Which model gives a greater probability of mass above 530 g?

slides.title: Different centers
slides.body: Model A is N(500,20). Model B is N(510,20), with mass in grams.
slides.question: Which model gives a greater probability of mass below 480 g?

slides.title: A probability or a cutoff?
slides.body: A manager asks for the mass exceeded by only 2% of packages.
slides.question: Does the requested answer have units of grams or units of probability?

slides.title: Conditional normal probability
slides.body: Model: X~N(500,20). A package is known to weigh more than 500 g.
slides.question: What is the probability that it weighs more than 520 g?

slides.title: A model boundary
slides.body: A normal model assigns some probability to every real-valued interval.
slides.question: When could its prediction of negative durations make it unsuitable for duration data?

slides.title: One package or an average?
slides.body: Model: independent package masses follow N(500,20).
slides.question: Should an average of 100 masses be analyzed using the same standard deviation as one mass?

slides.title: Checking an empirical normal model
slides.body: Synthetic durations (s): 8, 9, 9, 10, 10, 10, 11, 11, 12, 20. Fit a normal model using the sample mean and SD.
slides.question: How does its predicted proportion above 12 compare with the observed proportion?
